c11_chem_cbse_05_001: Van der Waals covers more than London forces — dipole-dipole counts, but H-bonds sit above them all. Check: how strong is it?
c11_chem_cbse_05_002: London forces act in every molecule, polar or not — and shape can beat molar mass. Check: linear or branched?
c11_chem_cbse_05_003: Electronegativity alone isn't enough — H-bonding needs the small size of N, O or F. Check: is the atom too big?
c11_chem_cbse_05_004: Boyle's law needs constant temperature — a heated gas won't follow PV = k. Check: did T stay put?
c11_chem_cbse_05_005: Celsius breaks the gas laws — convert to kelvin before you take ratios. Check: did you add 273?
c11_chem_cbse_05_006: Pick the R that matches your units — 0.0821 for L·atm, 8.314 for joules. Check: do the units cancel?
c11_chem_cbse_05_007: On mixing, each gas expands into the full volume — recompute each partial pressure. Check: did you apply Boyle per gas?
c11_chem_cbse_05_008: Graham's law carries a square root — rate ratio is √(M₂/M₁). Check: diffusion through gas or a pinhole?
c11_chem_cbse_05_009: Three speeds, three formulas — Graham's uses the average, the gas equation needs rms. Check: which speed does yours want?
c11_chem_cbse_05_010: Ideal behaviour fails at low temperature too — and at extreme pressure Z can top 1. Check: attraction or volume?
c11_chem_cbse_05_011: The correction adds to measured P and subtracts from measured V — not the reverse. Check: which sign went where?
c11_chem_cbse_05_012: Vapour pressure ignores how much liquid or headspace you have — temperature alone sets it. Check: did T change?
c11_chem_cbse_05_013: Surface tension and viscosity aren't twins — mercury beats glycerol on one and loses on the other. Check: one surface or two?
c11_chem_cbse_06_001: A sealed cooker still swaps heat — closed means matter stays in, not energy. Check: can heat cross?
c11_chem_cbse_06_002: Use ΔU = q + w — expansion work comes out negative. Check: what's w's sign?
c11_chem_cbse_06_003: Count only gaseous coefficients in Δn_g — liquid water doesn't make the cut. Check: which species are gases?
c11_chem_cbse_06_004: Formation equations build one mole of compound — and combustion ends at liquid water. Check: one mole of what?
c11_chem_cbse_06_005: Elements score zero only in their standard state — ozone and diamond don't qualify. Check: which allotrope?
c11_chem_cbse_06_006: Bond enthalpies are averages, and the broken-minus-formed trick needs gases. Check: all species gaseous?
c11_chem_cbse_06_007: Negative ΔG° doesn't mean total conversion — at equilibrium ΔG is zero, not the reactants. Check: ΔG or ΔG°?
c11_chem_cbse_06_008: q/T only counts on a reversible path — irreversible trips need a detour. Check: which path are you on?
c11_chem_cbse_06_009: Zero entropy needs a perfect crystal — frozen CO keeps residual entropy from random orientations. Check: is it perfect?
c11_chem_cbse_06_010: Only ΔG° ties to K — at equilibrium ΔG itself is zero. Check: are you at equilibrium?
c11_chem_cbse_07_001: Equilibrium isn't stillness — evaporation and condensation keep trading blows. Check: are the rates equal?
c11_chem_cbse_07_002: Equal rates don't mean equal amounts — equilibrium can sit at 85% product. Check: rates or concentrations?
c11_chem_cbse_07_003: Pure solids and liquids don't enter K — their activity is one. Check: did CaCO₃ sneak in?
c11_chem_cbse_07_004: Only gases count in Δn_g — and match R to your pressure units. Check: bar or atm?
c11_chem_cbse_07_005: In Q and K the coefficients become powers — 3H₂ means [H₂]³. Check: exponents or multipliers?
c11_chem_cbse_07_006: Adding a reactant shifts forward but never fully undoes it — the new level stays higher. Check: higher than original?
c11_chem_cbse_07_007: Pressure moves the position, never the constant — Kp holds at fixed T. Check: did Kp really change?
c11_chem_cbse_07_008: A catalyst quickens both directions equally — you reach the same yield sooner. Check: does K move?
c11_chem_cbse_07_009: A Bronsted base just accepts a proton — NH₃ qualifies without any OH. Check: who accepted H⁺?
c11_chem_cbse_07_010: Lewis acids aren't only octet-poor — cations and polar double bonds accept pairs too. Check: who accepts the pair?
c11_chem_cbse_07_011: Water stays out of Kb — its activity is one, so drop [H₂O]. Check: what are the units?
c11_chem_cbse_07_012: 10⁻⁸ M HCl can't give pH 8 — water's own ions matter. Check: did you count water's H⁺?
c11_chem_cbse_07_013: A buffer needs a weak partner — HCl plus NaCl won't buffer. Check: is the acid weak?
c11_chem_cbse_07_014: For Ag₂CrO₄ the silver term is squared — and a common ion starts at its added level. Check: where did Cl⁻ begin?
c11_chem_cbse_07_015: Write hydrolysis with the ion, not the salt — NH₄⁺ donates a proton to water. Check: which ion reacts?
c11_chem_cbse_08_001: Oxidation doesn't need oxygen — chlorine can oxidise sodium just as well. Check: who lost electrons?
c11_chem_cbse_08_002: An oxidation number is a counting tool — sulfur in SO₂ doesn't carry a real +4. Check: formal or physical charge?
